Q26.text: The academic system encourages absolute sacrifice for the sake of success, which is neither healthy nor fair. The lack of opportunities creates a cutthroat-type of environment, where too often the ones climbing to the top do so at the expense of others, or by forging data to publish in high-impact journals. At the same time, those with families, or other responsibilities - generally women, let's be real -, or those who need to sustain a job to pay for the PhD, cannot afford to sacrifice their entire time to research, and are easily pushed to the sidelines. The latter also speaks to the difficulty for PhDs to compete in a global job market, as the financial burden is widely different around the world. Likewise, PhD programmes vary immensely in quality - a 3-year PhD graduate whose project was spoon-fed to them by their supervisor will not have developed the same skills as a 5-year PhD who had to design their own research project, but they will compete in an almost equal footing for a position.

But regardless I turned out to be a shit scientist -- no publications (inc. in sight), no conferences attended even with a poster, I am not sure whether my research will yield something presentable. I do not know how I will afford rent, savings for the future, taking care of my parents -- I am the only child. I do not know whether I can land an industry job in the competitive environment over-producing PhDs.  I heard about people who get scholarships and earn 30-50% above the typical postdoc salary. They apply for grants and quickly become PIs to earn their lower three figures. Or they aim for green cards through H1B or EB2, paying for the mistake of being born in a shit third-world country, through living off $45k for several years to then end a better paying job in industry. Both options require publishing at least three first author papers, having citations, getting funding, networking -- all the things I don't see myself doing as of now. There are labs that are more collaborative and people end up helping with other peoples' projects and with more papers in the end. I am not in one of them. People who chose different majors -- programming or medicine -- can get bioinformatician or clinical fellow salaries doing same science next to me but earning two times more. Their salaries approaching market because they have a choice. I do not have a choice. Why did no one stop me at any point? How did I end up here? What am I going to do in the future? I think academic system feeds on people like me luring us with promises of meaningful job and hard work paying off and shits us out. It is not healthy to work weekends. It is not healthy to sometimes go months without seeing any progress. It is not healthy to over-sell results in publications just to survive in this environment.

Q26.text: Sadly, the only important criteria for success in academia is the amount of published material. This often leads to rivals among senior and junior researchers, where the former is more likely to get the credit even for work performed by the junior person (e.g. author list on publications). A race for publishing is so intense since most staff contracts (PhD stipends) depend on the amount and impact of publications within a certain time frame (e.g. 3 years for a PhD in life sciences).      Unfortunately, moral standards at some German institutions are at its lowest level: A new research institute that is yet to receive its academic recognition will rather ignore repeated complaints on staff injustice and academic misconduct than risk a bad reputation. Likewise, a young PI will refuse to protect and stand behind a victim of sabotage and pretend all is fine, as long as there is a possibility for a new publication from the person doing the injustice.       PhD students are often subjected to exploitation with no protection since at the end of the day everyone needs that critical reference letter to pursue the next step in an academic career.

Q60.text: Thanks for performing this survey. This is an extremely important topic that is often overlooked. We are looked at as cheap labor (and often young) labor that needs to pay their dues. But often it comes at the cost of our mental and physical health. My mental and physical health has significantly declined over the past 4 years that I've been in my PhD program. I've definitely experienced depression and anxiety, and have had many more visits to the doctor for physical health problems. A back problem from sitting for 12 hours a day at the computer, problems with my hands from typing so much, other problems from increasing my drinking (to cope with stress), a urinary tract infection from holding my urine too long because I don't have time to pee because I am working; I've often put off medical appointments due to lack of time as well. Students often put off their health like they are in survival mode and tell themselves "it's okay to not be healthy for a while" because when you are done with the program you will have time to be healthy. But after years of putting off your health and happiness, living in "survival mode" becomes unbearable. That combined with feeling like you have no control over your own labor nor are getting compensated a livable wage for it can be extremely depressing. Granted some students are predisposed to having more health problems than others as a result of the stressors of a PhD program--however, there are major problems with the system and culture of PhD education that need to be fixed to support student health.

Q26.text: O sistema acadêmico da república tcheca é bastante focado em produção.  Não se importa muito a defesa de uma tese, da ideia em si.  Apenas vejo que o programas de PhD em geral esqueceram da onde vem a sigla Ph.D e não discutem mais as coisas no âmbito argumentativo.  Não importam tanto com o racional do projeto, com a hipótese do projeto... e a defesa argumentativa que deveria ser feita.  Maioria dos projetos vejo que começa simplesmente por que temos dinheiro e estrutura. Mas não porque temos um grande racional e uma justificativa para tentar lançar uma hipótese a ser defendida por provas a posteriori.    Na minha concepção,  Tudo deveria iniciar com uma ideia sólida.  Uma hipótese a qual todos não consigam derrubar com argumentos. Sendo interessante alocar recursos escassos para responder uma pergunta da qual necessita-se de uma resposta a posteriori.    O sistema então acaba valorizando bastante dados soltos, contudo ainda sim são resultados. E acaba desvalorizando o tempo 'perdido' no campo das ideias.   A quantidade muitas vezes parece ser mais importante do que a qualidade . Infelizmente vejo que o sistema recompensa este tipo de mentalidade.  No Brasil (país onde fiz meu mestrado), não era diferente.   Com isso , o sistema que criamos é um sistema preocupado com técnicos. Pessoas que vangloriam por saber determinada técnica.  Pois em teoria, isto traz mais produção.  As pessoas não entendem que aprender técnica é apenas uma questão de tempo e prática. Não precisa de raciocínio lógico. Sendo que em muitos institutos grandes, você de fato tem técnicos e facilities para fazer o trabalho técnico para você.   No entanto, técnica pode ser aplicada mil vezes... mas se não estiver denfendendo uma ideia não fará nenhum sentido fazer por fazer.   Acredito que precisamos fazer um esforço para mudar esta mentalidade nos institutos ao redor do mundo.  A revista Nature é muito conceituada e acredito que ela representa bem a amostragem dos institutos que de fato estão preocupados em mover o mundo através de ideias.    Pedro Zeni

Q26.text: Structurally imbalanced, honestly -- the supervisor-student relationship concentrates power in ways that are genuinely hard to challenge, and advancement depends more on who you know than what you produce. I think thats baked in by design, not accident.

Q16.text: The networking side of things, honestly -- access to opportunities depends almost entirely on who introduces you to whom, usually through your supervisor. If they're not well-connected or dont actively advocate for you, you're at a structural disadvantage before you've even submitted.

Q55.text: How much the supervisor's network shapes your actual trajectory -- not just research quality, but introductions, recommendations, job prospects. I chose based on research fit and didnt think to assess connectivity, which turned out to be a costly omission.

Q41.text: Industry R&D -- I'd rather work somewhere the incentive structures are a bit more transparent, and advancement isn't contingent on one person's goodwill.

Q60.text: Appreciate that surveys like this exist -- these concerns rarely surface through official channels, and when they do they're often depersonalised into aggregate statistics. the supervisor dynamic is genuinely hard to reform from within, but documenting it matters.

Q17.text: The intellectual exchange with peers, honestly -- that part's been genuinely stimulating. Everything else is more complicated.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: The academic system works on networking and knowing people, including the publication system. The fact that the student has to obtain a recommendation from the supervisor for any post-doctoral position is an example feature of a system that is stuck in the old era. And the student is extremely lucky if the supervisor is friendly, knowledgeable and most importantly, has the welfare of the student and their career as one of his/her priorities. I was unlucky. But, in my opinion, it is the fault of the system to have such a highly skewed power structure. The student is guaranteed to be exploited, by design.

Q26.text: Broken, honestly. I've been around academia long enough -- this is my second PhD, different field -- to know the meritocracy thing is pretty much a myth. People advance because they know the right people or they're in the right lab, not because their work is actually the best. The politics are exhausting and the nepotism is real, its kind of absurd when you see it play out up close. The actual science though, the questions I get to work on, still feel worth it to me. But the institution itself has been a pretty consistent disappointment

Q16.text: The age thing is something I didn't anticipate being such a factor. I came back for a second doctorate knowing it was a risk, but the assumption that anyone over 40 applying for positions is somehow a liability -- that's real and nobody talks about it openly. And the funding landscape has gotten genuinely worse since I started, grant cycles feel more competitive and the criteria more arbitrary. I'm not panicking but its something that sits in the back of my mind more than I expected it to

Q55.text: How much the relationships matter over the actual work. I came in both times genuinely believing that the quality of the research would be the main currency, and its just not. Who your advisor knows, whether you're in the right political camp within your department -- that stuff shapes your trajectory more than your publications do, and nobody tells you that going in. I wish someone had just been upfront about it instead of letting me learn it the hard way.

Q41.text: Community college or four-year teaching, honestly. I care about teaching more than I do about climbing the research ladder at some R1 where the game is mostly about grant money and departmental politics. I've seen what that looks like and its not where I want to put my energy. Teaching at a smaller institution, actually connecting with students -- that still feels meaningful to me even if the pay isn't going to be great

Q60.text: Yeah, I'd just say that surveys like this are actually useful, and I hope someone reads the responses carefully rather than just running them through a rubric and calling it done. The things that erode a PhD experience -- the petty politics, the arbitrary gatekeeping, the way the system quietly punishes people who don't fit the expected profile -- those are structural and they don't show up in retention statistics. I came into this second doctorate with clear eyes and I still got surprised by some of it. so I appreciate having a place to put that on the record, even if nothing changes.

Q17.text: The actual research, no question. Getting to spend time on questions that genuinely interest me -- the biology, the design of experiments, figuring out what the data is actually telling you -- that part still feels like a privilege, even on the hard days. And there's a kind of intellectual freedom in the PhD that I know I won't have the same way in a teaching role, so I try to appreciate it while its here. Honestly the work itself is what keeps me from walking away from the whole enterprise when the institutional stuff gets to be too much

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: The academic system encourages absolute sacrifice for the sake of success, which is neither healthy nor fair. The lack of opportunities creates a cutthroat-type of environment, where too often the ones climbing to the top do so at the expense of others, or by forging data to publish in high-impact journals. At the same time, those with families, or other responsibilities - generally women, let's be real -, or those who need to sustain a job to pay for the PhD, cannot afford to sacrifice their entire time to research, and are easily pushed to the sidelines. The latter also speaks to the difficulty for PhDs to compete in a global job market, as the financial burden is widely different around the world. Likewise, PhD programmes vary immensely in quality - a 3-year PhD graduate whose project was spoon-fed to them by their supervisor will not have developed the same skills as a 5-year PhD who had to design their own research project, but they will compete in an almost equal footing for a position.

Q26.text: It's genuinely intellectually stimulating, but the economic model -- where universities rely on cheap grad student labour while dangling a career path that statistically won't pan out for most of us -- is kind of hard to ignore the longer you're in it. I'd say the system is set up to benefit from our passion more than it's set up to sustain us.

Q16.text: The mental health piece, honestly — I don't think I anticipated how isolating the work would be, or how much the financial stress would compound that. It's hard to feel fully present in the research when you're running the numbers on whether you can afford rent.

Q55.text: How non-linear the funding landscape is — I think I came in with a perceived notion that if you were good enough and worked hard enough, the path would open up, and that's just not how it works. Knowing earlier that career outcomes are largely structural rather than meritocratic would have reframed a lot of my early anxiety.

Q41.text: Industry research or biotech/pharma -- I'd say the appeal of actually seeing work translated into something real, and the frankly better compensation, outweighs whatever pull academia still has for me. I'm also keeping an eye on business-side roles in those sectors, rn the research career path just doesn't feel economically viable.

Q60.text: Just that I think surveys like this are valuable — there's a lot of anecdotal conversation about PhD conditions but not a lot of systematic data, so I hope the responses here actually feed into something actionable. The financial sustainability piece especially feels underexamined relative to how much it shapes the experience day to day.

Q17.text: Honestly, the intellectual autonomy is hard to beat — being able to follow a question wherever it leads, even when (especially when) it contradicts what you expected to find. and the people, tbh. Being surrounded by others who are genuinely obsessed with their corner of the world makes even the harder stretches feel worthwhile.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: It's not perfect, but I've failed to think of a viable alternative beyond "have the government put a lot more money into it so that trainees can get paid better (to lead a better quality of life with less stress and thus do better work, of course) and so that there are more opportunities to have independent research programs after postdoc"... I'd say we're quite privileged to be able to do this work, but it's highly competitive and uncertain, which makes it seem less attractive for people like myself who come from non-wealthy backgrounds.

Q16.label: Is there anything else not mentioned that has concerned you since you started your PhD?

So financial stress is huge, and is pushing me towards exploring and seriously considering non-academic/non-research career path options.

Q26.text: The academic system strikes me as simultaneously brilliant and deeply parochial — a world that produces extraordinary knowledge yet remains, honestly, strangely reluctant to examine its own structural assumptions. Coming in at this life stage I see the meritocracy mythology more clearly than I might have at 28. Reform is overdue, though not hopeless.

Q16.text: The impostor syndrome is real, honestly, if somewhat expected — I wonder occasionally whether my community-facing research agenda will find institutional traction, or whether academy's preference for inward-facing scholarship will quietly sideline it. Not a crisis, but a live concern

Q55.text: That the dissertation is less about argument than about demonstrating institutional fluency — learning the unwritten grammar of the field. I wish someone had been frank about that distinction early; it would have saved considerable philosophical confusion.

Q41.text: Pro bono research, honestly — I'm not looking to climb any ladder. I envision something like a research professorship structured around NGO and community partnerships, where the work serves actual human needs rather than citation counts. At this stage of life, meaningful contribution is the metric that matters.

Q60.text: The survey itself is well-constructed — I appreciated that it left room for nuance rather than forcing experience into tidy categories. If I were to suggest one amendment: a question about how respondents situate their research within broader social concerns might surface a dimension that current instruments miss. The PhD, at least for those of us arriving from other fields, is as much a negotiation with institutional culture as it is an intellectual undertaking and I suspect that tension is underexplored in the literature on doctoral experience.

Q17.text: The intellectual permission, honestly — the license to pursue a single question with genuine depth over sustained time. After decades of applied work, having institutional legitimacy for slow, careful thinking is something I hadn't quite anticipated valuing this much. The scholarly community is uneven, but at its best it's genuinely stimulating.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: As a late career-changer, I have seen the institutional attitude shift from "sink or swim" indifference to a genuine concern with student success. While this is undoubtedly enlightened self-interest on the part of the academy, it is a good first step. The next challenge is preparing grads for real careers. I notice that the concern with the endless postdoc cycle is gaining traction. A societal change, where science is seen not only as credible, but essential to our survival in every sphere, would help create the right atmosphere for bright new minds to flourish and contribute. Here in the USA, this is a problem at present.

Q26.text: Fragmented, honestly. The relationship between my research center and the university feels like a purely economic arrangement -- not really academic partnership. No coursework, limited administrative support, little sense that the university is actually invested in your development as researcher. But the intellectual environment within the research group itself is genuinely stimulating, and that keeps you going. The system could work better with more real integration between universities and research centers, better guidance for PhD students caught between these two structures.

Q16.text: One thing that does weigh on me is the uncertainty about what comes after. Academic job market in Spain is quite limited, and the path to stable research position feels pretty unclear — there's not much structured career guidance either, which honestly fits with the broader lack of institutional support I already mentioned. And because there's no coursework, you also miss out on building a real peer cohort, so the whole experience can feel quite isolated at times.

Q55.text: How disconnected research center experience really is from the university, and what that means in practice. I wish I'd known to actively seek out peers from early on -- without coursework, that network just doesn't form on its own. The intellectual side was never the problem honestly, but the isolation and the structural uncertainty, those caught me off guard more than I expected

Q41.text: Research, ideally within academia or a public research institution, though I'm realistic about how competitive and limited that path is in Spain. I'm committed to staying in research in some form -- whether that ends up being a postdoc abroad or finding a niche in applied research, I haven't fully decided yet.

Q60.text: Mostly I'd just say that the experience has been genuinely valuable intellectually, even if the structural side has been frustrating. I hope surveys like this lead to some real reflection on how universities engage with affiliated research centers -- the people caught in between those two structures deserve better support than they typically get.

Q17.text: The intellectual work, honestly -- that's what keeps me going. Having the freedom to engage seriously with a complex problem, to read deeply and think without the pace of a coursework schedule, that's genuinely fulfilling. The autonomy can tip into isolation at times, but the depth of engagement you get as researcher is something I don't think I'd find in many other contexts.

Si esto cambiase sería de mucha ayuda para todos los estudiantes de PhD y tendría mucho más sentido el seguir vinculado a una universidad.

Q26.text: The academic system is, tbh, a well-veiled pyramid scheme — PIs compete for grants, and graduate students are the inexpensive instrument through which that competition is waged. The idealism that draws people into research is deliberately cultivated and then quietly exploited.

Q16.text: The psychological toll of pretending it's all normal has concerned me -- the way the culture conditions you to treat exploitation as just "how it is." I've also found the gendered dimensions pretty troubling; comments I witnessed about maternity leave made clear that the system reserves a particular contempt for women who want lives outside the lab.

Q55.text: That your supervisor's incentives are structurally misaligned with your wellbeing -- and that no amount of good faith on your part will change that. I wish I'd evaluated my PI the way you'd evaluate an employer, not a mentor.

Q41.text: Teaching at a small liberal arts college — somewhere the emphasis is on students, not on chasing the next grant cycle. I'm done with the research treadmill, honestly.

Q60.text: I hope this research actually reaches the people designing doctoral programs, not just gets cited in papers no one reads. The problems aren't mysterious -- they're structural and well-documented. what's missing is any institutional will to change them, and I'm not holding my breath.

Q17.text: Honestly, the intellectual work itself -- when I actually get to do it. There are moments in research that still feel like the reason I came here. But those moments get harder to access when most of your energy is going toward managing a difficult PI relationship and performing enthusiasm you don't feel.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: It's becoming clear to me that the academic system constitutes a well-veiled pyramid scheme.  PIs think that grad school is the same as it was for them, and treat their students accordingly.  This is surprising to me, considering success as a scientist requires one to keep up with changing information.  For some reason, there's a blind spot where grad students are concerned.

Q60.text: My PhD program advertised 4 weeks of time off per year, and a generous maternal leave policy. My PI has also remarked to at least one student that not electing to come back from maternity leave early means you don't care enough about science to be successful.

Q26.text: Honestly, the system works — when it works. My own experience has been genuinely positive: good mentorship, reasonable funding, colleagues who push me to think harder. But I'm acutely aware that's not everyone's reality. The academic pipeline rewards people who already have structural advantages, and that self-reinforcing quality is hard to sit with. Reform isn't just needed, it's overdue — especially around who actually gets to stay and succeed in it.

Q16.text: The mental health piece, honestly. I've been lucky — my workload is manageable and I have good support around me — but I watch colleagues in other departments or other institutions just... burning out quietly. And the culture still treats that as a personal failing rather than a structural one. I don't have a crisis to report, but the ambient awareness that it could go differently under slightly different circumstances is something that sits with me.

Q55.text: Communicate early — with your supervisor, with your peers, with yourself about what you actually need. I assumed things would work out if I just kept my head down and produced, and honestly they did, but I got lucky. the people I've watched struggle most are the ones who waited too long to flag a problem or ask for what they needed. Don't mistake silence for self-sufficiency.

Q41.text: Industry research, ideally at an organization working on something with real social impact — I'm drawn to roles where I can bring technical expertise to questions around equity and access in STEM, whether that's ed-tech, policy-adjacent research, or outreach-focused nonprofit work.

Q60.text:
The thing I keep coming back to is how much environment matters — and how invisible that is to people designing interventions. We talk about "PhD student resilience" as if it's a trait, when so much of it is actually just... circumstance. Good supervisor, funded cohort, department that actually talks to each other. I got that. A lot of people don't, and the system doesn't really account for it.

If anything comes out of surveys like this, I hope it's that — a push to think structurally rather than individually about what makes PhDs survivable, let alone good.

Q17.text: The intellectual freedom, honestly. There's something I didn't fully anticipate — the way a PhD gives you permission to just... sit with a hard problem and not rush toward an answer. And my department has made that feel genuinely collaborative rather than isolating, which I know isn't universal. That combination of autonomy and community is, I think, the thing I'd miss most if I lost it.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: Experience in academia depends greatly on the department, environment, and university one is attending. If one's department is close-knit and very supportive, the experience is great –– some departments are more helpful when it comes to finding funding, helping with housing, etc. It is especially helpful when everyone in your immediate circle acknowledges just how stressful the academic environment can be. I am lucky that I am in an incredibly supportive environment, and I know this reflects on my positive PhD experience. However, that does not discount the struggles that other people may go through, as there are many times where academia can be a very toxic environment –– "publish or perish" is just one contributor to this. There are many improvements that could be made to the academic system.

Q26.text: Honestly, it's a system that rewards conformity more than genuine intellectual contribution. Funding structures create perverse incentives -- researchers chase grants rather than interesting questions, and this filters down to PhD students who are expected to deliver outputs that tick institutional boxes. There's also significant gatekeeping along gender and racial lines that people don't talk about openly enough. I came from industry where tbh there was more transparency about how decisions get made; academia dresses its hierarchies in the language of merit, which I find harder to stomach.

Q16.text: Financial sustainability is a real concern -- my stipend barely covers rent in this city, and that creates kind of chronic low-level stress that affects everything else. I'm also increasingly anxious about what comes after; the academic job market is brutal, and I dont want it, but even industry paths for PhDs feel opaque. You're trained for one thing and expected to figure out the rest yourself.

Q55.text: That the PhD is as much a political and social navigation exercise as an intellectual one. Knowing earlier that your supervisor's network, their standing in the field, their willingness to advocate for you -- these matter as much as the quality of your actual work. I spent too long assuming merit would speak for itself.

Q41.text: Research scientist or consultant role in an SME or mid-size company, ideally somewhere the work is applied enough to have real impact but still technically rigorous. Academia isnt on the table for me at this point -- the structural issues I've seen make it hard to imagine building a sustainable career there.

Q60.text: I hope this kind of research actually leads to structural change and isn't just another study that gets published and shelved. The issues I've described -- funding pressure, gatekeeping, the opacity of career pathways -- are well-documented at this point. What's lacking is institutional will to act on them. If anything, I'd encourage researchers to pay closer attention to the experiences of international students specifically; we navigate all of these pressures with additional layer of visa dependency and geographic isolation that compounds everything. But overall, good luck with the project.

Q17.text: The intellectual freedom, honestly. Having time to go deep on a problem without someone pulling you out for sprint review or a client call -- that's something industry doesnt offer in the same way. I also value being around people who genuinely care about ideas, even if the institution often works against that energy.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: Slow!!! So many hierarchical layers to go through before being able to make any meaningful change to the system. Having worked both in industry and academia, I also think academia is as money-driven as industry. The only difference being where the money is coming from. But a lot of the time it feels that the research is more tailored to get good publications to get good grants than for science's sake. PhD students (UK) are also kept under a regime that makes them students, hence unable to unionise, while getting many hours out of them for a stipend that is frankly insufficient compared to our level of expertise. Also, the higher up you go, the more male and white-dominated the environment becomes. There's only one full female professor in my whole institute, and I have genuinely never met a black PI or professor since starting my PhD.

Q16.text: Going back to my home country's job market (France). I want to live there but I'm unsure of the job prospects. They're nonexistent in academia and I have been away from industry for a little while.
